newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices reverse early Nigeria, Iraq-based gains.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices reverse early Nigeria, Iraq-based gains.

text.p: World oil prices fell late on Tuesday, reversing early gains triggered by the possibility of lower oil exports from Nigeria and heightened tension between Iraq and the United States.

Dealers said the underlying market tone remained soft and some expected a resumption of the three-month downtrend over the next few days. Weakness in the nearby crude futures contract on the New York Mercantile Exchange, which expires on Tuesday, also weighed on the market.

Bellwether London Brent crude futures for June delivery closed 35 cents lower at $17.99 a barrel, well down from the morning high of $18.64 but still above the nine-month low of $17.54 hit about three weeks ago.
The downdraft in oil prices has been severe since January when prices touched nearly $25 a barrel. Last year the average for Brent was $20.32 a barrel.
But on Tuesday prices were lifted early by a threat to Nigerian oil exports. Operators Shell said there would be delays loading tankers but that no cancellations were expected.
Royal Dutch Shell Group's Nigerian unit said it had declared force majeure on export of Bonny crude oil because of a strike by contractors that handle the berthing and loading of tankers.
Meanwhile, Iraqi helicopters arrived safely at Iraq's southern border with Saudi Arabia to pick up Moslem pilgrims, the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) said on Tuesday.

The White House on Monday urged Iraq to reconsider, saying it would "respond appropriately" to any such flights. U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said Iraq could not flout no-fly rules by arbitrarily sending helicopters to pick up the pilgrims, but it might be eligible for a humanitarian exemption allowing the flights if it followed proper procedure.

"I'm not very impressed by this market. The helicopters are pretty insignificant and Nigeria is a perennial problem," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of the oil division at Bankers Trust International in London.

Prices had also found support on Monday from news that OPEC's president Libyan Oil Minister Abdalla el-Badri had called on the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries' members to restrain output to help support sagging crude prices.
"The president has been calling and asking members to exercise restraint," OPEC Secretary-General Rilwanu Lukman told Reuters on the sidelines of an industry conference here.
"We will have to wait and see," whether member countries would respond, Lukman added.

OPEC output, estimated in a Reuters survey at 26.90 million barrels per day in March, has risen by about a million barrels per day (bpd) in the past year and is approaching two million bpd above the group's official 25.03 million ceiling.
Unseasonably cold weather in the key heating oil market of the Northeast United States has also been helping support prices, traders said.
Although more normal temperatures are expected soon, a seasonal pick up in gasoline demand is expected in the United States.
